## Claims

### Fourth text/comment — Enoch (14–16)

**C1.** Green classifies Jude 14–16 as the fourth “text” and comment unit in the series on the heretics’ coming (cf. vv. 5–7, 9, 11), with comment parallel to vv. 8, 10, 12–13.  
- Quote: “In these verses, Jude introduces his fourth “text” regarding the coming of the heretics (cf. vv. 5–7, 9, 11), which he then comments on as he did with the previous references to the OT narrative (vv. 8, 10, 12–13).”  
- Locus: L1767

**C2.** Green holds this unit is “the most problematic text-and-comment section” because Jude quotes 1 Enoch directly rather than referring to the OT; it is the only place Jude quotes a pseudepigraphic text (prior angelic-fall material in v. 6 is traditional reference, not quotation).  
- Quote: “This, however, is the most problematic text-and-comment section of the series since Jude quotes 1 Enoch directly to make his case instead of referring to the OT. He previously referenced traditional material regarding the angelic fall (v. 6), but this is the only place where he quotes a pseudepigraphic text.”  
- Locus: L1767

**C3.** Green states Jude’s purpose with the Enoch text is continuous with the letter: predicted coming, corrupt character, and final judgment of the heretics.  
- Quote: “The way Jude utilizes and comments on this passage is in complete harmony with his purposes up to this point: to show that the coming of the heretics was predicted, as also their corrupt character and final judgment.”  
- Locus: L1767

**C4. [jude-1-enoch-canon / authority]** Green’s core position: Jude does **not** treat the 1 Enoch quotation as less authoritative than the previous “texts.”  
- Quote: “He does not treat this “text” as any less authoritative than the previous ones (see “Jude and Pseudepigraphic Literature” in the introduction).”  
- Locus: L1767

**C5.** Green outlines the unit as (a) Text: prophecy of Enoch (14–15); (b) Comment: these are grumblers, complainers, and boastful flatterers (16).  
- Quote: “a. Text: The prophecy of Enoch (14–15)” / “b. Comment: These are grumblers, complainers, and boastful flatterers (16)”  
- Locus: L1773, L1775

**C6.** Green identifies Jude’s fourth “text” as a **direct quotation** from 1 En. 1.9, not an allusion to ancient biblical narrative.  
- Quote: “Jude’s fourth “text” section in this epistle is not an allusion to ancient biblical narrative (cf. vv. 5–7, 9, 11) but rather a direct quotation from 1 En. 1.9.”  
- Locus: L1786

**C7.** Green notes the biblical Enoch of Gen. 5:18, 21–24 (not Cain’s son, Gen. 4:17–18); later biblical focus is faith/translation (Heb. 11:5; Sir. 44:16; 49:14), while Jude emphasizes Enoch’s prophetic role.  
- Quote: “Later biblical comment on the Enoch story focused on his faith and the fact that he was taken up by God (Heb. 11:5; cf. Sir. 44:16; 49:14), while Jude emphasizes his prophetic role.”  
- Locus: L1786

**C8.** Green describes 1 Enoch as a composite document, strands roughly fourth century BC to the beginning of the Christian era; preserved in Aramaic (Qumran), Greek, Ethiopic, with fragments in other languages.  
- Quote: “We cannot be certain of the precise date when this book was composed, but it is likely a composite document that drew together strands dating from between the fourth century BC and the beginning of the Christian era (for a summary, see E. Isaac, OTP 1:6–7).”  
- Locus: L1788

**C9. [jude-1-enoch-canon / authorship]** Green denies historical Enochic authorship of the book: Enoch was not the author of this pseudepigraphic work, and it is not likely to preserve material from that historic personage.  
- Quote: “Enoch was not the author of this pseudepigraphic work, and it is not likely that the book preserves material from that historic personage.”  
- Locus: L1790

**C10. [jude-1-enoch-canon / relation to Scripture]** Green argues 1 En. 1’s primary motifs (divine theophany, universal judgment, salvation for the righteous) find their counterpart and source in Scripture; the book “does not present an independent witness of these events but relies on and interprets scriptural sources.”  
- Quote: “Moreover, all the primary motifs in 1 En. 1 find their counterpart and source in Scripture, including the divine theophany, universal judgment, and salvation for the righteous. … The book does not present an independent witness of these events but relies on and interprets scriptural sources.”  
- Locus: L1790

**C11. [jude-1-enoch-canon / quotation formula]** Green treats Προεφήτευσεν … as an introductory formula paralleling NT use for OT prophets whose prophecies are fulfilled in the present (Matt. 11:13; 15:7; Mark 7:6; 1 Pet. 1:10; etc.).  
- Quote: “In the NT, the declaration that someone “prophesied” is an introductory formula used to refer to OT prophets whose prophecies are being fulfilled in the present time (Matt. 11:13—the Law and Prophets; Matt. 15:7 and Mark 7:6—Isaiah; 1 Pet. 1:10—OT prophets; and cf. Jer. 25:13; Acts 2:16; and see Fitzmyer 1960–61: 303).”  
- Locus: L1792

**C12. [jude-1-enoch-canon / rejects Charles]** Green rejects J. Charles’s attempt to make “prophesied” more general (like Paul’s “prophet” for a Cretan in Titus 1:12): Titus calls Epimenides “their very own prophet,” whereas Jude says “Enoch … prophesied” and places the text with other authoritative texts (vv. 5–7, 9, 11, 17–18).  
- Quote: “J. Charles (1991a: 144) attempts to show that “prophesied” here may mean something more general than classifying 1 Enoch as a prophetic book: “And if, by way of illustration, a Cretan is to the apostle Paul a ‘prophet’ (Titus 1.12), then Enoch, in Jude 14, can ‘prophesy.’” However, in Titus 1:12 Paul calls Epimenides “their very own prophet.” Jude, on the other hand, says “Enoch . . . prophesied” and places this “text” together with other authoritative “texts” (vv. 5–7, 9, 11, 17–18) in his quest to outline the heretics’ sin and doom.”  
- Locus: L1792

**C13. [jude-1-enoch-canon / rejects opponents-authority thesis]** Green rejects the view that Jude quotes 1 Enoch merely because his opponents considered it authoritative (contra J. Charles 1991a: 144; Moo 1996: 273).  
- Quote: “There is no indication here that he simply quotes 1 Enoch because his opponents considered it to be authoritative (contra J. Charles 1991a: 144; Moo 1996: 273).”  
- Locus: L1792

**C14. [jude-1-enoch-canon / authority language]** Green concludes nothing in Jude’s language or the book’s context suggests Jude viewed this “text” as anything other than authoritative.  
- Quote: “Nothing in his language or in the context of the book suggests that he viewed this “text” as anything other than authoritative.”  
- Locus: L1792

**C15. [jude-1-enoch-canon / not like Paul’s classical citations]** Green places Jude’s use **outside** the category of Paul’s quotations of classic authors (Aratus/Cleanthes, Acts 17:28; Menander, 1 Cor. 15:33; plus Titus 1:12): Jude regards 1 Enoch as prophecy predicting present events and binds it with previous denunciations (“But Enoch also”).  
- Quote: “Jude’s use of this text is not in the same category with Paul’s quotations of classic authors (Aratus and Cleanthes in Acts 17:28; Menander in 1 Cor. 15:33; in addition to Titus 1:12). He regards 1 Enoch as a prophecy that predicts present events and binds this “text” with his previous denunciations of the heretics: “But Enoch also” (δὲ καὶ . . . Ἑνώχ, de kai . . . Henōch).”  
- Locus: L1794

**C16. [jude-1-enoch-canon / rejects Charles on “also”]** Green rejects Charles’s suggestion that “But Enoch also” points to the opponents’ high regard for the source: that “does not square with the way Jude frames the quotation.”  
- Quote: “Charles’s suggestion that these words point to his opponents’ high regard for his source does not square with the way Jude frames the quotation.”  
- Locus: L1794

**C17.** Green cites Clement of Alexandria on the passage: “In these words he [Jude] verifies the prophecy.”  
- Quote: “Clement of Alexandria commented on this passage, “In these words he [Jude] verifies the prophecy.””  
- Locus: L1794

**C18.** Green holds that what was prophesied is now fulfilled; the “remote generation” of 1 En. 1.2 is Jude’s generation; τούτοις = “about these” (or possibly “to them,” Bigg).  
- Quote: “Under either reading, what was prophesied is now viewed as being fulfilled. The “remote generation” of which Enoch spoke (1 En. 1.2)[3] is Jude’s generation.”  
- Locus: L1794

**C19.** Green notes “seventh from Adam” matches Gen. 5 genealogy and comes from 1 Enoch itself (60.8; 93.3; cf. Jub. 7.39); the designation highlights the significance of the following words against the heretics.  
- Quote: “The designation “the seventh from Adam” comes from 1 Enoch itself (60.8; 93.3; cf. Jub. 7.39, “the seventh in his generation”). … Identifying Enoch in this manner highlights the significance of the following words: no less than the seventh from Adam spoke against these heretics!”  
- Locus: L1796

**C20. [text form of 1 Enoch]** Green surveys the Greek-vs-Aramaic source debate; finds considerable duplication with Greek 1 En. 1.9, so Jude “knew the Greek text very well”; omissions/transpositions may be reworking or memory quotation; conscious modifications include christological “the Lord” coming (= Christ’s parousia).  
- Quote: “The considerable amount of duplication of the Greek form of 1 En. 1.9 argues strongly in favor of the position that Jude knew the Greek text very well. … There are clear indications that Jude made conscious modifications of his source since only in Jude’s version do we find that “the Lord” is coming, giving the quotation a christological orientation. He understands the passage to refer to Christ’s parousia.”  
- Locus: L1818

**C21.** Green notes traces of Aramaic knowledge: added “Behold!” (Ethiopic/Latin; possibly Aramaic); aorist ἦλθεν vs present ἔρχεται; “his holy myriads” closer to Aramaic/Ethiopic than Greek “his myriads and his holy ones.” He rejects Jude composing his own translation from Aramaic (contra Bauckham 1983: 96), while admitting uncertainty.  
- Quote: “The high degree of similarity between the Greek of 1 Enoch and Jude’s version points away from the view that Jude composed his own translation from Aramaic (contra Bauckham 1983: 96), although certainty once again eludes us.”  
- Locus: L1818

**C22.** Green: Jude transforms a divine theophany text into a reference to Christ’s advent; “Lord” is Jesus Christ (vv. 4, 17, 21, 25); high Christology—Christ’s coming and judgment anticipated; aorist ἦλθεν with future sense (possibly Semitic prophetic perfect); “holy myriads” = angelic host (Deut. 33:2 etc.), accompanying Christ at return.  
- Quote: “Jude has taken a passage that speaks of a divine theophany and has transformed it into a passage that refers to the advent of Christ (Osburn 1977: 334): … Jude’s high Christology is evident in this passage since Christ is the one whose coming and judgment are anticipated.”  
- Locus: L1820

**C23.** On v. 15, Green: “execute judgment” and “convict” describe Christ’s judicial acts; “this rebuke condemns; it is no longer educative”; Jude “appears to hold no hope of any redemption for the heretics.”  
- Quote: “Jude appears to hold no hope of any redemption for the heretics. In Christ’s coming, they will be judged and condemned.”  
- Locus: L1824

**C24.** Green stresses universal/comprehensive judgment of godless deeds and hard words; ἀσέβεια cluster recalls v. 4 and anticipates v. 18; “hard” speech as substantive (some MSS add λόγων—additional note L1849); charge amounts to blasphemy “against him,” essence of denying “our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ” (v. 4).  
- Quote: “This is the essence of the sin of the heretics who “deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ” (v. 4 NRSV).”  
- Locus: L1828 (see also L1826)

**C25.** Comment v. 16: pejorative “these”; heretics as γογγυσταὶ μεμψίμοιροι—grumblers (exodus typology, v. 5) and malcontents; living κατὰ τὰς ἐπιθυμίας; mouths speak ὑπέρογκα (echo As. Mos./T. Mos. 7.9, not inflated flattery—contra Neyrey); flattering for gain (θαυμάζοντες πρόσωπα ὠφελείας χάριν); avarice theme from v. 11; church not of extremely modest means if attracting such flatterers.  
- Quote: “Jude’s point here is not that they spoke “inflated words of flattery” (Neyrey 1993: 79). He rather shines his spotlight on their arrogant speech, which is characteristic of those figures in apocalyptic literature who stand against God.”  
- Locus: L1840 (see L1832–1844)

**C26. [text-critical, v. 15]** Some Greek MSS add λόγων (א, C, 33, 81); weight favors exclusion; Green includes “words” in translation as understood.  
- Quote: “15. Some Greek MSS add λόγων (א, C, 33, 81), although the weight of the evidence favors its exclusion. The thought, however, is understood in the expression τῶν σκληρῶν ὧν ἐλάλησαν . . . ἁμαρτωλοὶ ἀσεβεῖς and, hence, included in my translation: “hard words that godless sinners have spoken.””  
- Locus: L1849

### Apostolic prophecy (17–19)

**C27.** Green: vv. 17–19 close the text/comment cycle (vv. 5–19), forming an inclusio with the call to “remember” (v. 5a // v. 17 μνήσθητε).  
- Quote: “The present verses bring to a close the cycle of text/comment sections of the book (vv. 5–19), which were introduced with the call to “remember” (v. 5a) and are now brought to conclusion with the same call in verse 17 (μνήσθητε, mnēsthēte), thus forming an inclusio (envelope) around this section.”  
- Locus: L1857

**C28. [authority of apostles]** Green: turning to apostolic prophecy about the end “elevates the apostolic word to the level of his other authoritative texts.”  
- Quote: “Jude’s “texts” have ranged through the OT and apocryphal literature. But he now turns to apostolic prophecy about the end and, in doing so, elevates the apostolic word to the level of his other authoritative texts.”  
- Locus: L1857

**C29.** Green: “But you, beloved” (as v. 3; again v. 20) draws a sharp line between heretics (“these are,” v. 16) and the church; distances them from those who deny “our Lord Jesus Christ.”  
- Quote: “Here Jude draws a sharp line between the heretics, introduced with Jude’s characteristic “these are” (v. 16), and the church, “But you, beloved.””  
- Locus: L1857

**C30.** Green: call to remember is moral exhortation to heed and act—not mere information—to contend for the faith (v. 3) via building up (vv. 20–21) and rescue (vv. 22–23).  
- Quote: “Throughout the text/comment section, Jude’s purpose has not been merely to inform his readers of the heretics’ error and end, but especially to persuade the “beloved” to have nothing to do with them and their ways, a point made explicit in the following section (vv. 20–23).”  
- Locus: L1878

**C31.** Green: τῶν ῥημάτων τῶν προειρημένων = prophetic message “previously spoken”; as ancient judgment was decreed (v. 4), so apostles prophesied their coming; Jude’s point is fulfillment now present—pesher applied to the apostolic oracle.  
- Quote: “In reminding his readers about this prophecy, Jude’s point is not to prepare them for what is yet to come but rather to demonstrate that events predicted have now already come to pass. Jude interprets the apostolic oracle as he does his other “texts”: Now is the time of fulfillment. This is pesher exegesis applied to the apostolic oracle: Now is the time of fulfillment (on pesher interpretation, see “Genre and Structure” in the introduction).”  
- Locus: L1880

**C32.** Green: apostles likely from the restricted group (Paul and the Twelve); šālîaḥ model—“The one sent by a man is as the man himself”; their word is Christ’s, so the following “text” has Christ’s authority.  
- Quote: “The prophetic “text” that follows is invested with nothing less than Christ’s authority.”  
- Locus: L1882

**C33.** Green: no exact NT parallel for the prophecy except 2 Pet. 3:2–3, which Green’s introduction argues was penned using Jude; may be paraphrase/summary with possible redactional “ungodliness”; method cannot be demonstrated with certainty.  
- Quote: “The prophecy that Jude cites in this verse has no exact parallel elsewhere in the NT, save for 2 Pet. 3:2–3, which, as argued in the introduction to 2 Peter (see “The Relationship between 2 Peter and Jude”), was penned using Jude. … It may well be that Jude paraphrases rather than quotes the apostolic prophecy in mind, summarizing and perhaps even modifying the wording (not necessarily the thought) to show its applicability to the present situation.”  
- Locus: L1884

**C34.** Green: “to you” (ὑμῖν) most simply means the readers had heard the apostolic witness (not only a general word for all churches); if Palestinian, plausible contact with Twelve/Paul given Jude’s status.  
- Quote: “However, absent any indication from the context that this was a general word for all (like the Enoch prophecy in v. 14, which is introduced similarly but without “to you”), we should understand the dative pronoun in the simplest way: they had heard the apostolic witness.”  
- Locus: L1886

**C35.** Green: “last time” is present reality begun with Christ’s advent, not distant future; heretics’ presence indicates the last time has arrived.  
- Quote: “Jude, as these other NT authors, envisions the “last time” not as an era in the distant future but as a present reality, which has begun with the advent of Christ (see Acts 2:17; 1 Cor. 10:11; Gal. 4:4; Heb. 1:2; 9:26; 1 Pet. 1:20). … The presence of the heretics themselves is an indicator that this “last time” has arrived.”  
- Locus: L1888

**C36.** Green on ἐμπαῖκται: scoffers who despise morality/religion; dishonor via hubris frame (Aristotle; Josephus on Chronicles); charge serious without need to detail content of mocking (cf. 2 Pet. 3:3–4).  
- Quote: “Jude has no need to detail the content of their mocking (cf. 2 Pet. 3:3–4). The charge, taken from the apostolic prophecy, is enough to demonstrate how degraded the heretics were.”  
- Locus: L1892

**C37.** Green: prophecy language of living by godless desires is identical with v. 16 charge—suggests Jude had the apostolic prophecy in mind when writing that comment; stitched to Enoch section via ἀσέβεια (vv. 4, 15).  
- Quote: “The language of the prophecy is identical with the charge in verse 16 (see comments), which suggests that Jude had the apostolic prophecy in mind when he penned the previous “comment.” … The apostolic prophecy is again stitched to the preceding text/comment section (vv. 14–16), thus doubling the impact of the charge against the heretics.”  
- Locus: L1894

**C38.** Comment v. 19: heretics cause divisions (ἀποδιορίζοντες); some persuaded, others wavering (vv. 22–23); tear community vs building up (v. 20).  
- Quote: “Their end was to tear asunder the community instead of building up the believers together (cf. v. 20 and comments).”  
- Locus: L1898

**C39.** Green: ψυχικοί = “worldly/natural” people, not governed by the Spirit (1 Cor. 2:14; 15:46–49; Jas 3:15); “devoid of the Spirit” means they are not even believers—“the ultimate cause of the heretics’ immorality.”  
- Quote: “To have the Spirit of God is to be a Christian, and not to have the Spirit is to be outside this state of grace. Jude reinforces his previous claim: These people are not even believers! … Within a Christian context, no accusation could be more devastating.”  
- Locus: L1904

**C40. [rejects second-century Gnostic frame]** Green: language does not presuppose second-century gnostic soulish/spiritual division; fully comprehensible mid-first-century; reading as table-turning of gnostic opponents would be anachronistic.  
- Quote: “In this verse, Jude’s language and accusation do not presuppose that his opponents were gnostics of the second century who divided the world between those who were “soulish” and those who were “spiritual.” … To do so would be anachronistic.”  
- Locus: L1906

### Exhortations (20–23)

**C41.** Green: vv. 20–23 are the final body section after the text/comment litany (5–19); community building (20–21) and redemptive rescue of the swayed (22–23); apostasy real, hope if deliberate action; danger of being taken in.  
- Quote: “Apostasy is a genuine threat, but even in the face of such ruin, Jude forwards hope if, indeed, the church takes deliberate action. This mission is, however, fraught with danger, so Jude warns the community not to be taken in by the immorality as they engage in this rescue.”  
- Locus: L1926

**C42.** Green treats participles (building, praying, eagerly awaiting) as equivalent to imperatives alternating with τηρήσατε (BDF §468.2; Daube on 1 Peter).  
- Quote: “But it is more likely that Jude, like Paul, alternates between participle and imperative … considering the participle as an equivalent of the imperative (BDF §468.2; and see D. Daube’s appended note, “Participle and Imperative in 1 Peter,” in E. G. Selwyn 1946: 467–88).”  
- Locus: L1945

**C43.** Green: ἐποικοδομοῦντες ἑαυτούς = corporate building for unity against division (v. 19), not merely individual growth; construction metaphor a topos urging unity (Mitchell); foundation = “your exceedingly sacred faith” (superlative ἁγιωτάτῃ), the once-for-all handed-down faith of v. 3.  
- Quote: “Jude is not merely exhorting the individual believer to grow in faith but also calls the church to labor together for its corporate growth, which certainly integrates and benefits each particular member (implied in ἑαυτούς, heautous, yourselves; see Eph. 4:11–16). … Community is the soil where faith grows.”  
- Locus: L1947

**C44.** Green on prayer “in the Holy Spirit”: contrasts with Spirit-less heretics (v. 19); marks true people of God; rejects (as primary sense) Bauckham/M. Green/Pentecostal reading as speaking in tongues—corporate struggle against heresy; word and Spirit define true community.  
- Quote: “Some have suggested that Jude may have in mind speaking in tongues (Bauckham 1983: 113; M. Green 1987: 200), an interpretation of the text that is especially well known in Pentecostal/charismatic circles. In this section, however, Jude’s concern is with the corporate life of the church in their struggle against heresy, and given the problems within the Corinthian church regarding speaking in tongues, it is hard to imagine how such a call would contribute to the church’s corporate life (see 1 Cor. 14:4).”  
- Locus: L1953

**C45.** Green on “keep yourselves in the love of God”: counters heretics’ pattern of not keeping proper place (angels v. 6; exodus v. 5; Sodom v. 7); indicative of being “kept” (v. 1) becomes imperative; “principal imperative is a powerful call to flee from apostasy.”  
- Quote: “This principal imperative is a powerful call to flee from apostasy.[2]”  
- Locus: L1959

**C46.** Green: eagerly await the eschatological mercy of the Lord Jesus unto eternal life; vivid parousia hope argues against Jude as “early catholicism”; mercy as final blessing opposite judgment; church’s mercy to the fallen (22–23) mirrors God’s act.  
- Quote: “The vivid hope of the parousia argues against the view that Jude is a representative of “early catholicism.” Eschatological expectation is linked with Christian ethics.”  
- Locus: L1961

**C47. [text-critical 22–23 — Green’s decision]** Green: 22–23 “undoubtedly one of the most corrupt passages” (Osburn); prefers shorter **two-clause** reading of 𝔓72 as original (oldest MS; shorter; explains others; Birdsall, Osburn, S. Winter, Bauckham et al.), against UBS4/NA27 three-clause majority.  
- Quote: “Since 𝔓72 is the oldest witness, and since it contains the shorter reading, is supported by other ancient witnesses, and best explains the origins of the others, the present commentary will consider the shorter two-clause reading to be original.”  
- Locus: L1973

**C48.** Green’s 𝔓72 sense: (1) “Snatch some from the fire” (echo Zech. 3:2; possibly Hebrew; fire = final judgment; apostasy possibility real); ἁρπάζω = forceful, swift rescue.  
- Quote: “For Jude, the possibility of apostasy was as real as the hope of redemption for those who have been taken in by the theology and the practices of the heretics.”  
- Locus: L1977

**C49.** Second group: διακρινομένους = “those who dispute” (as v. 9), not primarily “doubters”; not the heretics themselves (no redemption hoped for them; marked for condemnation from of old, v. 4); rather heretics’ disciples, combative, immoral; show mercy “in fear” of temptation (not primarily “fear of the Lord” here); “hating even the tunic stained by the flesh” echoes Zech. 3:4; sexual stain as metaphor for sin to hate while rescuing.  
- Quote: “They may be the heretics themselves (S. Winter 1994: 218; Bauckham 1983: 115), but this is unlikely since Jude has spoken of nothing but condemnation for them throughout the epistle. … But in the present verse, Jude instructs the church to “show mercy” on these who dispute.”  
- Locus: L1985 (see L1983, L1989–1993)

**C50.** Additional note on 22–23: three-clause (א A) vs two-clause witnesses; B a conflation of 𝔓72 and C; 𝔓72 supported by Clement Strom. 6.8.65, versions (itt syrph copsah), Jerome on Ezek 18; short reading difficult, hence clarifying expansions.  
- Quote: “Given this wide support, the antiquity of the MS witness, and the multiple variants witnessed in the other texts, the reading of 𝔓72 should be considered original.”  
- Locus: L2070

### Doxology (24–25)

**C51.** Green: Jude closes with doxology, not standard Hellenistic closing conventions; doxology-as-letter-closing a Christian innovation (Rom. 16:25–27; 2 Pet. 3:18; 1 Clem. 65.2, etc.), perhaps attributable to Paul; reflects oral reading in worship, without collapsing letters into homilies.  
- Quote: “Jude concludes his epistle with a doxology instead of the more-common Hellenistic letter-closing conventions. … This innovation to the letter genre appears to have Christian origins (Rom. 16:25–27;[2] 2 Pet. 3:18; 1 Clem. 65.2; Mart. Pol. 22.3; Diogn. 12.9), perhaps attributable to Paul (White 1986: 19).”  
- Locus: L2087

**C52.** Green (via Weima): four doxology elements—(1) recipient (dative, God, highly elaborated); (2) elements of praise (nominative: glory, majesty, might, authority); (3) time indication (most extensive: before all ages, now, for all ages); (4) Amen. Closing rehearses major letter themes (keep firm; stand blameless; common security/salvation; “through Jesus Christ” vs denial of Lord, v. 4).  
- Quote: “While the form of Jude’s closing is different from common letter closings of the era, it serves the same function of taking up the themes that were the major concern of the letter writer.”  
- Locus: L2093

**C53.** Green: hope of doxology is theocentric after forceful anti-heretic argument; God “able to keep you from stumbling” (φυλάξαι … ἀπταίστους)—protect from moral failure under heretics’ assault; apostasy not inevitable.  
- Quote: “Jude does not view the heretics as all-powerful nor does he believe that apostasy is the inevitable outcome of their assault.”  
- Locus: L2106

**C54.** Green: God able to make them stand before “his glory” blameless (ἀμώμους) with exceeding joy—final judgment scene; “his glory” is God’s presence, not the “glories” of v. 8 (against Clement’s angel reading); possible echo of 1 En. 104.1.  
- Quote: “Clement of Alexandria interpreted the clause as a reference to angels: “In the presence of His glory: he means in the presence of the angels.” But “his glory” should not be confused with the “glories” of verse 8. This is the glory of God … the manifestation of his presence”  
- Locus: L2110

**C55.** Green: “only God our Savior”—monotheism as foundation for worship more than polemic; “Savior” reassures “common security” threatened by heretics (v. 3); διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ most likely mediates ascription of glory (as Rom. 16:27), not “Savior through Jesus.”  
- Quote: “Most likely the latter is the case since the same construction appears in Rom. 16:27, where praise is raised “to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ” (NRSV).”  
- Locus: L2118 (see L2114–2116)

**C56.** Green: implied verb is indicative ἐστί(ν), not optative εἴη—attributes inherent to God; doxology carefully selects glory, majesty, might, authority (not random stereotypes; omits common “honor”); glory/majesty = honor/grandeur framing moral argument; might/authority = sovereign rule underwriting judgment theme; illocutionary imperatival force—“Adoration and ethics clasp hands.”  
- Quote: “These indicative statements about God’s authority and sovereignty have an imperatival illocutionary force. Adoration and ethics clasp hands.”  
- Locus: L2126

**C57.** Green: most extensive NT time formula—before all ages / now / for all ages; immutable attributes across past, present age, and eternity; Amen invites congregational affirmation of faith and commitment to God’s way alone.  
- Quote: “What is truly unique about Jude’s time reference is that it covers past, present, and future. … As the letter is read to the gathered believers, Jude’s hope is for the congregation to join in and recite the “Amen!” (1 Cor. 14:16; …), thereby affirming again their faith in this God and commitment to his way alone.”  
- Locus: L2130, L2132

### Additional Notes / text-critical (cross-unit)

**C58.** Green’s printed translation for 22–23 follows 𝔓72 two-clause form with critical-mark brackets, not the three-clause NA/UBS form.  
- Quote: “22–23⌜Snatch some from the fire. Demonstrate mercy, in fear, toward those who dispute, hating even the tunic stained by the flesh.⌝”  
- Locus: L1941

**C59. [jude-1-enoch-canon — synthesis of Green’s rejected alternatives]** Within this range, Green **rejects** or distances himself from: (a) “prophesied” as merely generic (J. Charles / Titus 1:12 analogy); (b) quotation only because opponents valued 1 Enoch (Charles; Moo); (c) “But Enoch also” as signaling opponents’ high regard (Charles); (d) classifying Jude’s use with Paul’s classical literary quotations; (e) Jude’s own full Aramaic translation as source (contra Bauckham 1983: 96). He **affirms**: equal authority with other Jude “texts”; introductory-prophecy formula; fulfillment/pesher; conscious christological editing of known Greek with possible Aramaic traces; motifs sourced in Scripture; non-Enochic historical authorship of the book.  
- Loci: L1767, L1790, L1792, L1794, L1818
